content.text: A model knows what its training data held up to a cutoff date, and it keeps answering long after that date with the same confidence. Code written for older library versions is part of that data, so assistants suggest deprecated APIs without any warning. Give the model current facts, versions and the date, and let tests catch what slips through.
A developer asks an assistant to add new rows to a pandas DataFrame in a fresh project. It answers instantly with
orders.append(new_rows, ignore_index=True)
and a short explanation. CI fails with
AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'append'
. pandas deprecated that method in 1.4 and removed it in 2.0, and the project runs a newer major version. The assistant never hinted that its answer might be out of date.
The common misconception
"An LLM knows the latest library versions and current facts unless it tells you otherwise." Developers come to expect this for good reasons:

items.text: Assistants often do know recent APIs, so the misses look like exceptions.
The tone never changes. A stale answer is written with the same assurance as a current one.
Some assistants search the web, so the same question is current in one tool and stale in another.
It's natural to assume a system would say "I'm not sure about the newest version" when it should.

content.text: The half-truth: a model may know a lot about recent releases, up to a point. It has no built-in signal for where that point is, and it doesn't flag the edge for you.
What actually happens
Knowledge stops at a cutoff
A model is trained on data collected up to some date, then frozen. Anthropic's models overview lists two dates for each model: a training data cutoff, the broader range of data used, and a reliable
knowledge cutoff

, the date through which its knowledge is most extensive and reliable. Anything after the training data cutoff is simply absent. And models stay in service long after it: the same page lists retirement dates for the current models that fall more than a year after their training data cutoff.

For a developer, that gap is concrete: a framework's next major version, a renamed configuration option, a security advisory published last month. None of it exists for the model until you put it in the context, and a question about it gets an answer about whatever the model saw last, delivered as if it were current.
The effective cutoff is fuzzier than the reported one
Cheng and colleagues, in
Dated Data

, probed models against versioned data and found that effective cutoffs often differ from the reported cutoffs, and can differ between resources and topics within one model. Two causes stood out: new web crawl dumps contain non-trivial amounts of old data, and deduplication of near-identical documents behaves in complicated ways. So even before the official cutoff, a model may have seen mostly older versions of a page.
Why the deprecated API wins

Wang and colleagues tested seven LLMs on code completion across eight popular Python libraries. All of them struggled with deprecated APIs, and the paper names two causes: deprecated usages are present in training data, which comes from open-source code without filtering for deprecation, and deprecation knowledge is absent at inference time. The surrounding code mattered a lot: inside functions written in the old style, 70% to 90% of completions used the deprecated API, against 9% to 18% inside up-to-date functions. Legacy code in your file invites legacy suggestions.
Nothing in the output marks it as stale

As earlier articles in this path showed, every answer is generated by the same next-token process. The model has no clock either: today's date reaches it only if your app puts it in the prompt. It can't compare its knowledge with a present it doesn't see.
The same task, old API and current API

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "total": [120, 80]})
new_rows = pd.DataFrame({"id": [3], "total": [50]})

# Common in code written before pandas 2.0:
orders = orders.append(new_rows, ignore_index=True)
# AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'append'

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "total": [120, 80]})
new_rows = pd.DataFrame({"id": [3], "total": [50]})

# DataFrame.append was removed in pandas 2.0; concat replaces it
orders = pd.concat([orders, new_rows], ignore_index=True)
print(len(orders))  # 3

content.text: The fix itself is one line. The point is where the knowledge came from: pandas' 2.0 release notes, not the model. Better still, put the facts the model lacks into its context. This script builds a system prompt from the versions actually installed and today's date:

blocks.code:
from datetime import date
from importlib.metadata import version

packages = ["pandas", "numpy", "scikit-learn"]
pins = "\n".join(f"- {name} {version(name)}" for name in packages)

system_prompt = f"""Today is {date.today().isoformat()}.
This project uses exactly these versions:
{pins}
Use only APIs that exist in these versions. If you are not sure that an
API exists in them, say so instead of guessing."""
print(system_prompt)

rows.text: The model knows the latest versions
It knows its training data up to a cutoff, then stays in use for months or years
If it's outdated, it will say so
Stale and current answers come out of the same process, with the same tone
Effective cutoffs often differ from reported ones and vary by source and topic
Only if your app puts the date in the prompt
A deprecation hint in the prompt is enough
In one study it wasn't; run the code and the tests

blocks.title: Give it current facts, not just a warning

content.text: State versions and the date in the system prompt, paste the changelog section that matters, or give the model a search tool. Anthropic's web search tool lets Claude use real-time web content beyond its knowledge cutoff, and citations are always included, so you can check which page an answer came from.
A deprecated API often still runs with only a warning: pandas 1.4 emitted a
FutureWarning
for
append
before 2.0 removed it. Code an assistant writes today can pass every test and break on your next upgrade. Treat deprecation warnings as errors in CI, for example with
python -W error::FutureWarning
How to apply it in your project
Keep a lockfile, and put the versions that matter, plus today's date, into the system prompt or the project instructions your assistant reads.
For anything that changes, such as APIs, prices or policies, supply the current documentation or enable a search tool instead of relying on memory.
Fail CI on deprecation warnings and run linters that know your library versions, so stale suggestions fail fast.

items.title: Check generated code against release notes when you upgrade

content.text: Before a major upgrade, search the codebase for APIs the release notes remove, including code an assistant wrote.
Key takeaways

items.text: A model's knowledge stops at a training cutoff, and the model keeps answering long after it.
Effective cutoffs are fuzzy and vary by topic, so recent releases may be thin or missing even before the cutoff.
Deprecated APIs are part of the training data, and nothing in the output marks them as old.
The model doesn't know today's date or your versions unless you put them in the prompt.
Ground the model with current docs and versions, and let tests and warnings catch the rest.
